config.title: Packaging & environments

intro.title: Packaging & environments
intro.body: In this lesson, you will learn how to create a simple Python package and manage its dependencies using a virtual environment. You will build a basic calculator package that includes functions for addition and subtraction, and you'll use a requirements.txt file to specify its dependencies. The core concepts covered are package structure, virtual environments, and dependency management with pip. By the end, you'll understand how to organize code into a reusable package and isolate project environments to avoid conflicts.
intro.usecase: Packaging and environment management are essential for developing reliable Python applications that can be deployed consistently across different systems. In real-world scenarios, data scientists use virtual environments to isolate dependencies for different machine learning projects, ensuring that libraries like TensorFlow or pandas don't conflict. Web developers package Flask or Django applications with requirements.txt files so they can be deployed on cloud platforms like AWS or Heroku without compatibility issues. Software teams use tools like pipenv or poetry to manage dependencies across development, testing, and production environments, preventing 'it works on my machine' lessons.

objectives: Construct a virtual environment to isolate project dependencies
Initialize a Python package with a setup.py configuration file
Configure package metadata including name, version, and dependencies
Implement dependency management using a requirements.txt file
Apply packaging commands to build distributable archives
Manipulate environment variables to control package behavior
Integrate external packages into your Python projects

steps.title: Add the if __name__ == '__main__' guard
steps.instruction: At the bottom of your file, add the standard Python module guard `if __name__ == '__main__':` and call your `main()` function inside it.
steps.hint: This ensures the main function only runs when the script is executed directly, not when imported as a module.
steps.analogousExample:
# Example of a module guard
if __name__ == '__main__':
    print('Script executed directly')
    main_function()
steps.expectedOutcome: Your script will have a proper entry point that executes the main function only when run directly.
successCriteria: The file ends with `if __name__ == '__main__':` followed by a call to `main()`.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both the `if __name__ == '__main__':` line and a call to `main()` indented under it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The module guard is missing or incorrect. Check that you have `if __name__ == '__main__':` with `main()` called inside.
